extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (especially Kantian aesthetics/teleology)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and characterizing Kant's criteria and conceptual distinctions for judging purposiveness, organisms, and the teleological explanation of nature as found in Critique of Judgment (sections on teleology, preformation/epigenesis, and physico-theology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mechanical and teleological causality
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature in its universal conformity to law (mechanical causality) is different from an Idea which limits it to a particular form (teleological causality); the latter is not comprehended by pure Reason and lies in a supersensible substrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical causality governs phenomena generally, but teleological causality is the form under which we must think organised beings (as purposes) because their internally purposive form contains no ground in mere mechanism. This distinction legitimizes using teleological principles when mechanical explanations are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasionalism (as teleological model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Cause furnishes immediately the organic formation on the occasion of every union of intermingling materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Occasionalism is assumed, 'all nature is quite lost' for philosophical inquiry, since it makes natural explanation superfluous; thus it is rejected for those doing philosophy. It implies many gratuitous supernatural interventions (anti-pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-established Harmony (as teleological model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Cause originally supplied capacities by means of which an organic being produces another of like kind, so species perpetually maintain themselves via nature's productive capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two readings: generations as educts (individual preformation/evolution) or as products (epigenesis). This model preserves natural mechanism while postulating original capacities rather than continual supernatural formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of individual preformation / evolution (preformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generations regarded as mere educts: individuals preformed from the beginning, development is merely unfolding of preexisting form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms: requires innumerable preformed beings, cannot accommodate hybrids, and tends toward excessive supernatural explanation if combined with Occasionalism. Advocates try to avoid full Occasionalism by preserving some natural development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of epigenesis / generic preformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Generations regarded as products: productive faculty of the generator contains the specific form virtually, and organisms are produced (epigenesis) rather than individually preformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favoured by Reason prior to empirical proof because it regards nature as self-producing rather than entirely dependent on continual supernatural formation; leaves most of organismal formation to natural mechanisms after an original organisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative impulse (Blumenbach's principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organised matter contains an undeterminable but unmistakable element called a formative impulse, distinct from mere mechanical formative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle admits a non-mechanical original organisation while still allowing natural mechanism to operate under higher guidance; Kant presents it as a necessary explanatory principle for organised matter without endorsing a full metaphysical account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: An organised being is a natural purpose insofar as its possibility (internal constitution) is represented through causality according to purposes; we can ask of it 'What is it for?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal purposiveness is bound up with an object's possibility as a purpose, and calls for teleological representation of its causality (design). It contrasts with merely mechanical objects that do not warrant such questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: External purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: One thing of nature serves another as means to a purpose; non-organised things can be externally purposive in relation to organised beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: earth, air, water serve as means for organisms. External purposiveness is different from internal; it is the relation of means to an end (usefulness) without implying that the thing itself is a purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only organised beings can be judged as purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Things that are not organised (e.g., mountains) cannot be regarded as means to purposes in the teleological sense because they contain nothing requiring a ground of possibility according to purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleological judgement applies specifically to organisms (natural purposes); attributing purposiveness to inanimate formations (mountains) is illegitimate in the same sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final purpose vs means (unconditioned purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: A final purpose is one that needs no other as condition of its possibility; external purposiveness indicates only means rather than final purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asking why something exists, we either attribute it to blind mechanism (no purpose) or to a designed ground. Only a final purpose would be unconditioned; natural things often function only as means rather than final ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity as candidate for ultimate purpose of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Man, as the only being capable of forming concepts of purposes and legislating ends (noumenally), may be judged the ultimate purpose of nature on earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant distinguishes between man as phenomenon (subject to natural destructive forces) and man as noumenon (moral being with freedom). Only the noumenal aspect allows man to be an unconditioned final purpose; this requires locating the ultimate purpose outside nature itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is not an adequate ultimate purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of happiness is a mutable Idea, projected under empirical conditions, and cannot serve as an unconditioned final purpose of nature because it is not determinate or attainable by nature consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness depends on empirical conditions and varying individual ends; nature cannot be expected to realize a universal, determinate happiness for humanity as an ultimate purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as ultimate purpose (production of aptitude for purposes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture (the production of the aptitude of a rational being to set arbitrary purposes in general and use nature as means) is the only state of human development that can be considered an ultimate purpose ascribable to nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture includes both skill (development of capacities) and discipline (freeing the will from despotism of desires). Culture is formal: it makes beings capable of being final ends themselves independently of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: culture of skill vs culture of discipline (training)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture of skill develops capacities for acting on purposes (technical/artistic/scientific skill); culture of discipline trains the will, freeing it from subjection to inclinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are necessary for humanity to become a final purpose: skill alone is insufficient because it does not secure free determination of the will; discipline (negative training) is required to make will independent of natural desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and political conditions for culture (civil community / cosmopolitan whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement of men's relations (lawful authority in a civil community) and, ideally, a cosmopolitan whole of states are formal conditions under which the greatest development of natural capacities (culture) can take place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inequality and division of labor enable skill development; lawful political order is necessary to harness freedom and prevent abuse of conflicting freedoms. Kant also controversially considers war as an instrumental, though undesigned, mechanism that may prepare states for lawful conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physico-theology (definition and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physico-theology is the endeavour of Reason to infer the Supreme Cause of nature and its properties from the empirical purposes of nature; it cannot disclose a final purpose of creation nor determine the Supreme Cause's full properties beyond empirical effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physico-theology can justify an idea of an intelligent World Cause only as a subjective concept for teleological judging; it cannot, by theoretical reason alone, establish theological properties or the final purpose of nature. Moral (practical) reason supplies an a priori Idea that physico-theology lacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral theology vs physico-theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral theology (ethico-theology) infers the Supreme Cause and its properties from moral purposes of rational beings (known a priori), whereas physico-theology proceeds from empirical purposes in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral theology is said to have primacy in establishing determinate concepts about a Deity adequate to teleological judging because it relies on a priori practical grounds, unlike physico-theology which is limited by empirical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealism of final causes / Pantheism (anti-explanatory alternative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some systems explain purposive unity by positing unity of inherence (one Substance) rather than causal design; this leads to pantheism/spinozism and effectively explains away purposiveness as mere misinterpretation of ontological unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such systems do not solve the question of the first ground of purposiveness but remove its reality by reinterpreting purposiveness as derivative from metaphysical unity, an approach Kant criticizes as inadequate for teleological explanation.
